13-17s: Tilts up as the ram trots fast around the base while amber light rises like wine inside the vessel, making the scale patterns glow gold.

24-30s: Pulls back to the opening angle as the ram springs into its corner and freezes into bronze; the zun stands whole and still, one last wink glinting.

subtitles.text: Hi! I'm one of the four rams on this bronze zun.
I'm about three thousand years old, from China's Shang Dynasty.
Long ago, I held wine for sacred ceremonies.
I was dug up in Hunan in 1938.
During the war, I was badly damaged, then repaired.
Now I live at the National Museum of China.

sources.fact: The bronze zun (wine vessel) with four ram-head sculptures dates to the Shang Dynasty (c.16th century-11th century BC).

Each of the four ram heads at the vessel's corners has a pair of curled horns, and there are four dragon heads between the ram heads. The whole surface is a shiny lacquer-black, in a clearly late Shang style.

The four ram-head sculptures at the corners and the fine patterns are described as a testimony to the superb bronze-casting technology of 3,000 years ago.

lines.text: Long ago, I held wine for sacred ceremonies.

sources.fact: The bronze zun (wine vessel) with four ram-head sculptures dates to the Shang Dynasty (c.16th century-11th century BC).

The Four-Ram Square Zun is a bronze from the earlier part of the late Shang dynasty. It is a ritual vessel and an object used in sacrifices. It is the largest square zun among surviving Shang bronzes in China, 58.3 cm high and weighing nearly 34.5 kg.
This zun was used in sacrificial ceremonies. It was unearthed in Ningxiang city, Hunan province in 1938 and was destroyed by bomb attacks during the war.

lines.text: I was dug up in Hunan in 1938.

sources.fact: This zun was used in sacrificial ceremonies. It was unearthed in Ningxiang city, Hunan province in 1938 and was destroyed by bomb attacks during the war.

According to research by Gao Zhixi, the Jiang brothers found the zun in 1938 and it disappeared during the war against Japan. It was found again in 1952, badly damaged, and was later restored. In 1959 it was transferred to the Museum of Chinese History.
